articles.headline_en: Meloni rival in AI scandal over edited photo that ‘undressed’ woman MP
articles.significance: The case illustrates how politically charged social-media posts using manipulated images can trigger accusations of sexism and public backlash.
articles.summary_en: Italian politician Roberto Vannacci was criticised after posting an AI-altered image of rival MP Matilde Siracusano that removed part of her clothing and exaggerated her cleavage. Vannacci said he had reposted the image from a blog and had not digitally altered it himself.[5]

articles.headline_en: Why are pictures of Italy’s Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani in a miniskirt going viral?
articles.significance: The episode shows how a politician’s comments about women’s clothing can become a major online controversy, prompting criticism and an apology.
articles.summary_en: Antonio Tajani faced online mockery and criticism from politicians and the Catholic Church after comments concerning the length of a woman’s skirt. Tajani subsequently apologised and said he had not intended to offend women.[8]

articles.headline_en: Police question 27 over election-day social-media posts
articles.significance: The investigation concerns the state enforcement of a legal blackout covering both paid political advertising and unpaid social-media posts.
articles.summary_en: Cyprus police questioned 27 people over more than 100 social-media posts and advertisements allegedly published during a period when election-related campaigning was prohibited. The investigation followed 127 complaints and includes OPEK president Theano Kalavana, whose post reportedly remained online; the restriction covers the eve of an election and polling day.[14]

articles.headline_en: Controversy over abortions – SDP MP deletes social-media post criticising the government
articles.significance: The reported deletion reflects the political sensitivity surrounding online claims about abortion-related fees and opposition criticism of government policy.
articles.summary_en: An SDP member of parliament deleted a social-media post criticising the government in a dispute over abortion-related client fees. The National Coalition Party accused the opposition of spreading false information about the fees.[3]

editorial_overview: The reporting gathered for the week shows several forms of politically consequential online speech. Individual politicians faced backlash over manipulated imagery and comments about women, while another legislator reportedly removed a post amid a dispute over abortion-related claims. In Cyprus, authorities are investigating social-media activity under a statutory election-period ban that applies to both paid and unpaid content. The available results provide limited evidence of court-ordered removals or direct platform moderation actions during the period.
topic: European press review: political speech, social-media controversies and online content controls, 23–30 September 2026
